newsitem.title: MALI: Mali opposition calls new poll protest for Monday.
newsitem.headline: Mali opposition calls new poll protest for Monday.

text.p: Opposition parties in Mali, which won plaudits for its 1992 democratic transition, have called a nationwide day of action for Monday to denounce electoral chaos and demand this year's polls be suspended.
The elections, which began with Sunday's problem-plagued parliamentary election, are the impoverished nation's second multi-party national polls since independence from France in 1960.

Two opposition alliances, whose supporters clashed with security forces in the capital on Wednesday, said in a statement afterwards that they would ask the constitutional court to scrap Sunday's results.
The government, for its part, said after a Wednesday cabinet meeting that it would maintain the electoral timetable but would respect any decision by the constitutional court.
"As in the past, (the government) will respect all rulings of the constitutional court on any issue submitted to it," a cabinet statement said.
Sunday's poll for a new 147-seat parliament and presidential and municipal elections in May and June are a test of how deeply democracy has taken root in the dirt-poor West African nation.
But many of the voters who flocked to the polls on Sunday found problems with voter cards, electoral lists or ballot materials prevented them voting.

Early results released by the Independent Electoral Commission (CENI), point to a lead for President Alpha Oumar Konare's ruling ADEMA alliance, which won a 1992 poll, but with many seats needing to go to an April 27 second round.

The opposition alliances, who represent 11 parties, want the results scrapped and say they will boycott the second round and the remaining elections. They have withdrawn their members from the CENI, calling for it to be reorganised.
Spokesman Mohamed Lamine Traore said that they had called their supporters to observe "a national day of democratic action" on Monday.
Police used tear gas to disperse protesters who tried to demonstrate in Bamako on Wednesday.
The two alliances, the opposition Front for Change and Democracy (FCD) and the Rally of Patriotic Forces (RFP) had denounced preparations for the elections before the poll.
The RFP includes supporters of the former single party and jailed former dictator Moussa Traore, whose 1991 overthrow cleared the way for democratic reform.
The FCD portrays itself as heir to the tradition of independence leader Modibo Keita, a nationalist and hardline socialist who declared a one-party state after independence.

Konare, a historian elected in 1992, has steered Mali on a course of economic liberalisation, winning praise from the United States and the World Bank. He had been due to face nine challengers for his job on May 4.
